extracted.intended_audience: criminalists, forensic investigators, judges, and legal practitioners involved in witness examination
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for forensic/criminological evaluation of witness testimony with emphasis on sensory illusions, perceptual errors, and psychological causes that affect reliability. Covers classification, examples, and practical signs to probe during examination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Passions may transmute into their opposites
rubrics_metrics.description: Under strong emotional circumstances passions and emotions often change into their opposites according to rule (e.g., parsimony becomes extravagance; love becomes hate; terror may become petrifying coldness).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When interpreting behavior or statements, investigators must allow that observable traits may reflect inverted emotional states; absence of 'typical' traits (e.g., lack of visible terror) can itself be a sign (e.g., icy indifference). Look for subordinate characteristics that accompany transformed passions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Passions carry subordinate characteristic clusters
rubrics_metrics.description: Passions carry a significant company of subordinate characteristics (e.g., dread or fear is accompanied by disorderly impertinence; sensuality by cruelty).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use knowledge of associated subordinate traits to explain or predict behavior and to generate leads about motive or personality. These associations may simplify explanations of criminal acts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Money exerts an overpowering, characteristic influence
rubrics_metrics.description: Money has the same definite influence on man as blood on preying animals; the sight of large sums can lead otherwise decent people to serious crimes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider the presence or sight of money as a possible proximal trigger or explanatory factor in crimes; use this tendency to identify motives and possible perpetrators when money is implicated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Honor is a social position that may persist in criminals
rubrics_metrics.description: Honor is simply the position a man takes with regard to the world; even criminals may retain notions of honor (e.g., the condemned prisoner asking to write farewell letters).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that 'honor' or concern for reputation can influence testimony and behaviour. Do not confuse pliability in interrogation with genuine honorable inclination, and avoid exploiting temporary decency to obtain confessions or accusations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criminals exhibit professional distinctions and pride
rubrics_metrics.description: Criminals may have professional ambitions and seek professional fame; what is proper for one class of offender (thief) may be improper for another (robber).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be attentive to intra-criminal social codes and professional pride when assessing motives, accusations against accomplices, or reputational complaints—these can produce strong reactions and explain unexpected behaviour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider superstition as an influencing factor
rubrics_metrics.description: Superstition can influence behaviour and should be considered in criminalist analysis (references provided to further discussion).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When relevant, investigate superstitious beliefs or ritual motives; consult the cited literature for detailed treatment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sensation is the basis of knowledge but is fallible
rubrics_metrics.description: Since sensation is the basis of knowledge, the sensory process is the basis of the correctness of legal procedure—but perception is not always completely correct and its mistakes must be studied.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat sensory testimony as potentially reliable but always subject it to scrutiny for known types of error. Familiarity with sensory illusion literature helps in identifying when testimony may stem from perceptual error.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classify perceptual states: normal, abnormal, and temporary somatic conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: A useful division of perception errors is into 'normal', 'abnormal', and a third class where somatic conditions (overloaded stomach, rush of blood to the head, wakeful night, over-exertion) favor or cause illusory perceptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When examining witnesses, assess whether conditions at the time (fatigue, recent exertion, indigestion, sleep deprivation) could have produced transient distortions and treat such testimony accordingly or seek medical input.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish real sensory illusions from false inferences
rubrics_metrics.description: Real illusions: the sense organ has registered wrongly (e.g., double vision from a displaced pupil). False inferences: sensations are correct but the conclusion drawn is wrong (e.g., seeing through a red glass and inferring the landscape is red).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Probe whether the witness’s error was in raw sensation or in inference/interpretation. Use cross-checks (other senses, instruments, alternate viewpoints) to separate sensory malfunction from mistaken reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correctness judged by constancy across conditions and observers
rubrics_metrics.description: A sense-impression is correct when it remains identical under various circumstances, in various conditions, when connected with other senses, and observed by different men, with different instruments; it is illusory when it is not so constant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seek corroboration of perceptual reports across times, conditions, observers, and instruments; lack of constancy is a warning signal of illusion or error.

rubrics_metrics.name: Investigators must actively seek out sensory illusions (witnesses rarely self-report them)
rubrics_metrics.description: Witnesses do not of course know that they have suffered from illusions of sense; the criminalist must seek them out.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask targeted questions to reveal conditions that produce illusions, look for internal inconsistencies, and when disease is possible, involve medical experts instead of relying solely on lay assessments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Optical positional effects: orientation and line position distort perceived size
rubrics_metrics.description: The position of lines influences estimation of size: perpendicular/vertical dimensions are taken to be somewhat greater; of two crossed lines the vertical seems longer; an oblong lying on its longer side may be taken as square, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat witness reports about size, extent, or inclination with caution—especially when judgments were made from a distance or at unusual angles. Use sketches, measurements, or on-site reenactments where possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Slight path deviations produce large distance/navigation errors
rubrics_metrics.description: Slight crooks are underestimated, producing systematic underestimation of distance and the curious fact that people lost at night often walk in a small circle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When witnesses or suspects report distances or routes travelled (e.g., fleeing into woods), allow for underestimated deviations; corroborate with physical evidence or trajectory analysis rather than relying on lay distance estimates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monocular bias: left/right eye underestimation
rubrics_metrics.description: The left eye sees objects on the left too small, while the right eye underestimates the right side of objects; this underestimation varies from 0.3 to 0.7%.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider small systematic lateral biases in size/location reports, particularly in poorly lit conditions or monocular viewing situations; where precise localization matters, test or note the viewing eye conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contextual cues (furnishing, snow, nearby known-sized objects) alter size perception
rubrics_metrics.description: An unfurnished room seems much smaller than a furnished one; a lawn covered with snow smaller than a thickly-grown one; size estimates are influenced by nearby objects whose size is known.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate the environmental context of observations—absence or presence of familiar size cues will bias witnesses. Use known-reference objects or measurements to recalibrate testimonies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Orifice and aperture effects on perceived size (keyhole/tube observation)
rubrics_metrics.description: The size of the orifice through which something is seen influences the perceived size of objects (Thomas Reid's moon example; observations through key-holes matter in criminal cases).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat observations made through small apertures (keyholes, peepholes, tubes) as unreliable for accurate size/distance estimation; reconstruct the viewing geometry when such testimony is critical.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aërial perspective and atmospheric conditions affect distance, color, and size judgments
rubrics_metrics.description: Atmospheric clarity, fog, and aerial perspective change the appearance of distant objects (colors and apparent size); conclusions about distance/size made under different weather conditions are unreliable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare witness-reported conditions (clear vs murky air) and prefer testimony made under similar atmospheric conditions; beware of mixing reports from observers who only saw the scene in different weather.

rubrics_metrics.name: Illusory lines / Zöllner-type juxtaposition effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Juxtaposition of inclined or crossing lines can make parallel lines appear unparallel and otherwise warp apparent shapes (Zöllner effects).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that complex patterns (ornaments, fabrics, carpet designs) or surrounding lines can create perceptual distortions; when witnesses describe angles or alignments, consider such visual-context illusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Figure-ground inversion and ambiguous figures cause bistable perception
rubrics_metrics.description: Visual inversion (e.g., a line seen as deeper or higher; cube corners seen as convex or concave) and ambiguous silhouettes (e.g., windmill arms appearing to move either way) can lead observers to a single, confident but potentially arbitrary interpretation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand that a witness’s confident assertion may reflect one stable interpretation of an ambiguous stimulus; ask whether alternate interpretations were possible and attempt to recreate viewing conditions to test ambiguity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Motion-related perceptual distortions (objects appear shorter during movement)
rubrics_metrics.description: During movement bodies can be distinguished only under definite conditions: moving objects seem shorter in the direction of movement and broader when slowing; viewing through a stationary small opening intensifies this.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be skeptical of precise size and shape judgments made while either the observer or the observed object was in rapid motion; use motion analysis or expert testimony for speed/size claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cross-modal timing and inference errors affect perceived sequence
rubrics_metrics.description: Because light and sound reach the observer at different times depending on distance, observers may infer a false temporal sequence (e.g., seeing the ax fall before hearing the blow or vice versa), leading to mistaken claims about order of events.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When sequence/timing is contested, account for physical delays between senses and consider geometric and acoustic factors; do not assume subjective simultaneity equals objective simultaneity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strangeness or missing expected cues undermines reliability
rubrics_metrics.description: If an event lacks expected logical developments (e.g., seeing a horse without hearing hoofbeats, a man without shadow), the perception becomes 'strange' and subsequently unreliable—the strangeness itself can magnify sensory error.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Probe witnesses for feelings of unease or that something was 'off'—these reports may indicate degraded reliability. Such subjective reports, even if understated, are diagnostically useful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Physiological and pharmacological states produce optical illusions
rubrics_metrics.description: Minor physiological disturbances (indigestion, local retinal inflammation) or drugs (morphine, cocaine) can cause strong optical illusions and color shifts (e.g., luminous black looks blue, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Always consider medical/drug factors when assessing testimony; consult medical experts and note signs of intoxication, withdrawal, or retinal/neurological disturbance that can produce perceptual distortions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Observer motion (e.g., train travel) alters perceived size, distance, and color
rubrics_metrics.description: When the observer is moving quickly (train, carriage), objects may seem too near, smaller, or colors may blend (green+red→white), producing systematic distortions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat reports made while the witness was in rapid motion with caution; where possible, reconstruct observations from a stationary vantage or simulate the observer’s motion to assess likely distortions.
